info.name: SealDoc
info.summary: Turn stored documents into evidence: PDF/A-3B, chain of custody, and a panel that says what is in each seal
info.description:
Nextcloud stores your documents. It does not, on its own, prove that a document has not changed since you filed it, or that it existed on the date you claim. For invoices, contracts and personnel records that have to survive a statutory retention period, that difference only becomes visible at the moment somebody asks, which is usually years later.
This app connects Nextcloud to SealDoc. Every document it processes comes back as a **PDF/A-3B** file validated against ISO 19005-3, together with an evidence pack: a **SHA-384 hash chain**, a **chain-of-custody** record and, where the SealDoc instance attaches one, an **RFC 3161 timestamp** from a trusted authority.
**How you use it**
- As a Flow (workflow) action: *when a file is created in /Invoices, seal it*. - Or one file at a time, from the row menu in Files. - The sealed file is written back next to the original, so it stays in the folder and the sharing you already have. - A shield marks sealed documents in the file list, and a **Seal panel** in the sidebar reports what that particular seal contains.
**It tells you what is missing**
The panel is not a row of green ticks. It reports each guarantee as present, absent or unknown, because a document can come back a perfectly valid PDF/A-3B with a complete chain of custody and no timestamp at all. A tick over a missing guarantee is worse than no panel, so a missing one is shown in red and named, with a sentence saying what it costs.
The shield in the file list follows the same rule and has three states, so you can see which documents will not hold up without opening any of them:
- a tick, where every guarantee is present; - an exclamation mark, where at least one is missing; - a question mark, where the seal could not be read back.
**What it does not do**
- It does not provide electronic signatures. It proves a document has not changed, not who agreed to it. Those are different questions. - It does not guarantee a timestamp. Whether one is attached depends on the SealDoc instance and its timestamping authority; the panel reports, per document, whether it actually got one. - Where a timestamp is attached it is an RFC 3161 timestamp from a trusted authority. It is **not** a qualified timestamp under eIDAS. - It does not decide how long anything has to be kept. An administrator can record the organisation's own retention policy, and it is shown as exactly that. - It is not an archive. It produces evidence designed to outlive the service; the file stays in your Nextcloud.
**Sealing runs as a background job**, so Nextcloud has to be set to run those on Cron. On the AJAX default a queued document can wait a long time or never be picked up; the settings page and the panel both say so rather than leaving you guessing.
**Where the processing happens**
You choose. Point the app at the hosted service in the EU, or at your own self-hosted SealDoc instance. The app talks to nothing else.
info.author: Bryan van Rijn
